title: 道德經 第三十四章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 34, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 69. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 34 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 任成 (Trusting to Fulfilment). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
大道氾兮，
其可左右。

morph.gloss: to spill over the banks and spread out flat — a river in flood
poetic exclamatory particle: nothing to translate, only a beat held open
it — here the bare subject of the clause, not the possessive 'its'
to left and to right — the standing pair for 'on this hand and on that', i.e. everywhere
the left hand, the left side
the right hand, the right side

sentences.l:
The great Way spills wide! —
it can go to the left and to the right.
sentences.i: The great Way spreads like a river in flood: it is there on the left hand and on the right.
sentences.n: 氾 is a rare character and a watery one: a river over its banks, spreading out across the flat. Wang Bi glosses it 汎濫無所不適 — spilling wide, with nowhere it does not get to — and adds that the Way may be used to left and right, above and below, turning every way, so that there is nowhere it fails to reach. 兮 is the poetic particle: it means nothing you can translate, it only holds the line open for a beat, and it is the mark of the older song-verse this book keeps reaching back toward. 左右 is bound here as the standing pair, 'on this hand and on that' — the two together mean 'every way', which neither gives you alone. That is the only place in the book where they stand side by side; chapter 31, full of lefts and rights, never puts them together, because there each is a separate ritual station and is glossed on its own.

sentences.t:
萬物恃之而生而不辭，
功成不名有。
衣養萬物而不為主，
常無欲，
可名於小；

morph.gloss: the ten thousand things — everything there is
to lean on, to depend on (in chapter 2's 為而不恃 the same character was 'presume upon')
to come to life, to be born
to decline, to beg off, to turn away — to refuse the trouble of them
the work brought off, what has been achieved; the credit for it
to be completed, brought to fulfilment
to name, to claim under one's own name — the noun 'name' used as a verb
to clothe (read yì as the verb; as the noun 'clothing' it is yī)
to feed, to rear, to keep alive
the lord, the master — the one in charge
in, among — marking the class a thing is placed in
the small (the adjective standing as a noun)

sentences.i: The ten thousand things depend on it for their life, and it turns none of them away; the work done, it puts no name of its own to the having. It clothes and feeds them all and never lords it over them; wanting nothing, ever, it may be counted among the small.
sentences.n: The first line all but repeats chapter 2 — 萬物作焉而不辭，生而不有 — with the Way standing where the sage stood there, which is one of the ways this book argues: the sage does what the Way does. The subject changes inside that first line with nothing to mark it: 萬物 are what lean and live, but it is the Way that does not turn them away. Only the sense tells you where the switch falls — this is the language's normal habit, not a difficulty in this line alone. 名 is a verb again, as it was in the first line of the book: 不名有 is 'does not put its name to the having', lays no claim. 衣 is read yì here, not yī — as a noun it is clothing, as a verb 'to clothe someone', and the reading follows the job the word is doing. And notice what the smallness rests on: not size, but that a thing which wants nothing and claims nothing gives you no hold on it, nothing to reckon as great. Wang Bi puts it so — all things are born of the Way and never know what they owe it, so that at the time of abiding desirelessness each thing has its own place and the Way looks as though it had bestowed nothing; and that is why it can be named in the small.

sentences.t:
萬物歸焉而不為主，
可名為大。

morph.gloss: to go back where one belongs, to come home
to it — 焉 here is the fusion of 於 'to' and 之 'it' in one syllable

sentences.l:
The ten-thousand things come home to it, and it does not act as their lord:
it may be named as great.
sentences.i: All things come home to it, and still it will not be their lord; so it may be counted great.
sentences.n: 焉 is doing the first of its two jobs here: the fusion of 於 'to, in' and 之 'it' into a single syllable, so 歸焉 is 'go home to it'. You have had the same fusion in chapter 2's 萬物作焉 and chapter 30's 荊棘生焉. Chapter 15's 豫焉 is the other job, where 焉 carries nothing but the fall of the line. The two units together are one argument in Wang Bi's reading: because everything is born of the Way and never knows what it owes, the Way can be counted among the small; because everything comes home to it and it still refuses to be lord, it can be counted great. The two namings are not written parallel — 名於小 'named in the small' against 名為大 'named as great' — and that unevenness is in the text, not in the English.

sentences.t:
以其終不自為大，
故能成其大。

morph.gloss: because of — 以其 opens the reason: 'because it ——'
to the end, at any point — with a negative: never
to make, to make out to be (wéi)
to complete, to bring to fulfilment
greatness (the adjective standing as a noun)

sentences.l:
Because to the end it does not make itself great,
therefore it can complete its greatness.
sentences.i: It is because it never at any point makes itself out to be great that it can bring its own greatness to completion.
sentences.n: 以 has been 'by means of' all through the book; here 以其 opens a reason instead — 'because it ——' — and the shape is chapter 7's exactly: 以其不自生，故能長生, because they do not live for themselves, therefore they can live long; and then 非以其無私邪，故能成其私. Once you know the frame 以其 … 故能 …, you can read the sentence before you have parsed it. 終 with a negative after it is 'never at any point', not 'in the end'. And 其 is back to the possessive it usually is — 其大, its own greatness — after standing as the bare subject 'it' in the chapter's opening line.
